LA-Loading components (34823045643) (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|Herbert Lehr (left) and Harry Daghlian Jr. (right), loading the assembled [[Tamper (nuclear weapon)|tamper]] plug containing the plutonium pit and initiator into a car for transport from the [[McDonald Ranch House|McDonald ranch house]] to [[Trinity (nuclear test)|the shot tower]] on July 13, 1945.]]

'''Haroutune Krikor Daghlian Jr.''' (May 4, 1921 – September 15, 1945) was an American [[physicist]] involved in the [[Manhattan Project]], which designed and produced the [[atomic bomb]]s that were used in [[World War II]]. He accidentally [[Irradiation|irradiated]] himself on August 21, 1945, during a [[critical mass]] experiment at the remote Omega Site of the [[Los Alamos Laboratory]] in [[New Mexico]] and died 25 days later from the resultant [[radiation poisoning]].

Daghlian was irradiated as a result of a [[criticality accident]] that occurred when he accidentally dropped a [[tungsten carbide]] brick onto a 6.2&nbsp;kg [[pit (nuclear weapon)|bomb core]] made of [[plutonium–gallium alloy]]. This core, subsequently nicknamed the "[[demon core]]", was later involved in the death of another physicist, [[Louis Slotin]].

==Early life and education==
Haroutune Krikor Daghlian Jr., was born in [[Waterbury, Connecticut]], on May 4, 1921, one of three children of Margaret Rose (''[[Birth name|née]]'' Currie) and Haroutune Krikor Daghlian. His father was an ethnic [[Armenians|Armenian]] from [[Gaziantep]], [[Turkey]]. He had a sister, Helen, and a brother, Edward.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1945-09-19 |title=Article clipped from The Day |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-day/130926121/ |access-date=2024-07-01 |work=The Day |pages=11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Howard |first=Lee |title=A death in the desert that 'Oppenheimer' ignored |url=https://www.theday.com/local-news/20230826/a-death-in-the-desert-that-oppenheimer-ignored/ |access-date=2024-07-01 |website=www.theday.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Soon after his birth the family moved across state to the coastal town of [[New London, Connecticut|New London]]. He was educated at Harbor Elementary School, where he played violin in the school orchestra, and at [[Bulkeley School|Bulkeley High School]]. In 1938, at the age of 17, he entered the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], intending to study mathematics,<ref name="nl-man-1st-victim">{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1915&dat=19850806&id=DiBSAAAAIBAJ&pg=2472,1066749 |title=NL man was 1st victim of atomic experiments |first=Paul |last=Baumann |newspaper=[[The Day (New London)|The Day]] |date=August 6, 1985 |pages=1, 4 |access-date=August 15, 2015 }}</ref> but became interested in physics, particularly [[particle physics]], which was then emerging as an exciting new field. This interest led him to transfer to the [[West Lafayette, Indiana]], campus of [[Purdue University]], from which he graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1942. He then commenced work on his doctorate, assisting [[Marshall Holloway]] with the [[cyclotron]]s. In 1944, while still a graduate student, he joined [[Otto Frisch]]'s Critical Assembly Group at the [[Los Alamos Laboratory]] of the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.atomicheritage.org/profile/harry-daghlian |title=Harry Daghlian |publisher=Atomic Heritage Foundation |access-date=August 15, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150830000707/http://www.atomicheritage.org/profile/harry-daghlian |archive-date=August 30, 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1915&dat=19410401&id=aA5HAAAAIBAJ&pg=4139,18903 |newspaper=[[The Day (New London)|The Day]] |date=April 1, 1941 |page=3 |title=Harry Daghlian, Jr., wins Purdue honor |access-date=August 15, 2015}}</ref>

==Criticality accident and death==
During an experiment on August 21, 1945, Daghlian was attempting to build a [[neutron reflector]] manually by stacking a set of {{convert|4.4|kg|adj=on}} [[tungsten carbide]] bricks in an incremental fashion around a plutonium core. The purpose of the neutron reflector was to reduce the mass required for the plutonium core to attain criticality. He was moving the final brick over the assembly, but neutron counters alerted Daghlian to the fact that the addition of that brick would render the system [[critical mass|supercritical]]. As he withdrew his hand, he inadvertently dropped the brick onto the center of the assembly. Since the assembly was nearly in the critical state, the accidental addition of that brick caused the reaction to go immediately into the [[prompt critical]] region of neutronic behavior. This resulted in a [[criticality accident]].<ref name="review">{{Citation |last1 = McLaughlin |first1 = Thomas P. |last2 = Monahan |first2 = Shean P. |last3 = Pruvost |first3 = Norman L. |last4 = Frolov |first4 = Vladimir V. |last5 = Ryazanov |first5 = Boris G. |last6 = Sviridov |first6 = Victor I. |date = May 2000 |title = A Review of Criticality Accidents |place = [[Los Alamos, New Mexico]] |publisher = [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] |pages = 74–75 |id = LA-13638 |url = http://www.orau.org/ptp/Library/accidents/la-13638.pdf |access-date = April 21, 2010 |url-status = live |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927235352/http://www.orau.org/ptp/Library/accidents/la-13638.pdf |archive-date = September 27, 2007 }}</ref><ref name="Sullivan 2016 p. 14-16">{{cite book | last=Sullivan | first=Neil J. | title=The Prometheus Bomb: The Manhattan Project and Government in the Dark |location=Lincoln | publisher=[[University of Nebraska Press]] | year=2016 | isbn=978-1-61234-890-2 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Md4nDwAAQBAJ | access-date=November 30, 2021 | pages=14–16 }}</ref>

Daghlian reacted immediately after dropping the brick and attempted to knock the brick off the assembly without success. He was forced to disassemble part of the tungsten-carbide pile in order to halt the reaction.<ref name="Millerp68"/>

Daghlian was estimated to have received a dose of 510&nbsp;[[röntgen equivalent man|rem]] (5.1&nbsp;[[Sievert|Sv]]) of [[neutron radiation]], from a yield of 10<sup>16</sup> [[nuclear fission|fission]]s.<ref name="review"/> Despite intensive medical care, he developed symptoms of severe [[radiation poisoning]], and his sister and mother were flown out to care for him.<ref name="nl-man-1st-victim"/> He fell into a coma and died 25 days after the accident.<ref name="Millerp68">{{cite book |last=Miller |first=Richard L. |title=Under the Cloud: The Decades of Nuclear Testing |publisher=Two Sixty Press |location=[[The Woodlands, Texas]] |year=1991 |isbn=0-02-921620-6 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/underclouddec00mill/page/68 68, 69, 77] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/underclouddec00mill/page/68 }}</ref><ref name="Sullivan 2016 p. 14-16"/> He was the first known fatality caused by a criticality accident. His body was returned to New London, where he was buried at [[Cedar Grove Cemetery (New London, Connecticut)|Cedar Grove Cemetery]].<ref name="A quiet victim of a horrific war he helped end" />

File:Partially-reflected-plutonium-sphere.jpeg|The sphere of [[plutonium]] surrounded by neutron-reflecting [[tungsten carbide]] blocks in a re-enactment of Daghlian's 1945 experiment<ref name="review"/>

==Legacy==
As a result of the incident, safety regulations for the project were scrutinized and revised. A special committee was established to review any similar experiments and recommend appropriate safety procedures. This change of procedures included needing a minimum of two people involved in such an experiment, using at least two instruments monitoring neutron intensities with audible alerts, and preparing a plan for operating methods and any contingencies that might occur during similar experiments.<ref name="accidents-1956">{{cite report |last=Hayes |first=Daniel F. |date=August 1956 |title=A Summary of Accidents and Incidents Involving Radiation in Atomic Energy Activities, June 1945 through December 1955 |place=[[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]] |publisher=[[United States Atomic Energy Commission|U.S. Atomic Energy Commission]] |pages=2–3 |id=TID-5360 |url=http://www.osti.gov/scitech/servlets/purl/4343762|doi=10.2172/4343762 |osti=4343762 |access-date=August 8, 2015|hdl=2027/mdp.39015095051879 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

These changes did not prevent another criticality accident from happening at Los Alamos the following year. [[Louis Slotin]], a colleague of Daghlian, was killed in 1946 while performing criticality tests on the same plutonium core.<ref name="review"/> After these two incidents it became known as the "[[demon core]]",<ref name=third>{{cite web |title=The Third Core's Revenge |publisher=Restricted data blog |last=Wellerstein |first=Alex |url=http://blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2013/08/16/the-third-cores-revenge/ |access-date=April 4, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407081649/http://blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2013/08/16/the-third-cores-revenge/ |archive-date=April 7, 2014 }}</ref> and all similar criticality experiments were halted until remote-controlled assembly devices were more fully developed and available.<ref name="accidents-1956"/>

In 2000, the city of New London erected a memorial stone and flagpole in Calkins Park to honor Daghlian. His surname is misspelled "Daghiian" on the monument. The monument bears an inscription: "though not in uniform, he died in service to his country."<ref name="A quiet victim of a horrific war he helped end">{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1915&dat=20000608&id=t5pGAAAAIBAJ&pg=1792,1497197 |date=June 8, 2000 |title=A quiet victim of a horrific war he helped end |first=Steven |last=Slosberg |newspaper=[[The Day (New London)|The Day]] |page=C1 |access-date=August 15, 2015}}</ref>
